# Ontology Playground (Preview) ☕

[English](README.md) · [简体中文](README.zh-CN.md) · [日本語](README.ja.md)

> Note: This project was developed with AI-assisted coding.

**[Try it live → microsoft.github.io/Ontology-Playground](https://microsoft.github.io/Ontology-Playground/)**



A free, open-source web application for learning about ontologies and
**Microsoft Fabric IQ**. Explore pre-built ontologies, design your own in a
visual editor, export as RDF/XML, and share interactive diagrams — all from a
fully static site with zero backend dependencies.






## Features

Text and icons use theme-aware foreground colors, including yellow accents in
the welcome, help, data-source, and quest panels. Automated contrast checks
cover the supported theme palettes.

### Interactive Graph Exploration

Cytoscape.js-powered graph that renders any ontology as an interactive
node-and-edge diagram. Pan, zoom, click nodes to inspect properties, and use
the live search bar to filter entities and relationships.
The graph has an accessible text summary naming the ontology and its entity
and relationship totals; semantic overviews also identify the visible counts.
Zoom, fit, reset, and PNG download controls have explicit accessible names,
while the legend and semantic-view controls remain independently accessible.
This summary does not provide keyboard navigation of canvas nodes.

### Ontology Catalogue

A curated library of official and community-contributed ontologies spanning six
domains (Retail, E-Commerce, Healthcare, Finance, Manufacturing, Education).
Browse by category, search by name or tags, load any ontology with one click,
and inspect or download its exact reviewed RDF source.
Catalogue cards preserve and display available license, upstream source, and
version attribution for external standards and adapted community entries. The
gallery downloads a lightweight metadata index; each versioned graph payload
and original source is published separately at an immutable,
content-addressed URL and verified by SHA-256 when requested. Original files
remain byte-for-byte intact, including source-only SHACL rules and unsupported
triples. The graph is a visual projection; opening a catalogue entry in the
Designer carries the complete verified source with it. Every ontology has a
shareable deep link
(`/#/catalogue/official/cosmic-coffee`).

### Visual Ontology Designer

A full-screen, split-pane editor for creating ontologies from scratch or
editing existing ones. Add entity types with icons, colors, and typed
properties; define relationships with cardinalities; see a live graph preview
that updates as you work, including reconnecting edges when a relationship's
From or To entity changes without repositioning existing nodes.
Includes undo/redo (50 levels), real-time validation,
and export to RDF/XML or JSON. Source-backed RDF uses a bounded editing mode:
only unambiguous existing labels, comments, and direct named-class
`rdfs:subClassOf` edges can be changed. Unsupported controls stay read-only,
and undo/redo updates both the graph projection and RDF statement patches
atomically. Editable literals retain their exact language, datatype, and graph
identity across successive edits, including when another literal has the same
text. Source-backed documents stay in this complete mode even when they have
no projectable classes, so authored starter templates cannot silently replace
their preserved graph. Ontologies with 1,000 or more projected graph elements
remain available in the viewer but are not opened in the all-at-once Designer.

### RDF Import & Export

RDF/XML imports retain the exact original bytes and a complete semantic graph
alongside the Playground's visual projection. Untouched downloads are
byte-for-byte identical, including BOM, encoding, formatting, and unsupported
statements. After a supported edit, export serializes the complete patched
graph rather than regenerating only the visible subset; all unrelated
statements remain present. Undoing every net edit restores exact-original
download eligibility.

The complete parser retains named and blank nodes, arbitrary predicates,
literal lexical forms, language tags, datatypes, OWL restrictions, RDF lists,
SHACL statements, and distinct RDF 1.2 directional language literals.
Directional language and text direction survive complete-graph edits and
serialization without collapsing `ltr` and `rtl` values. Standalone RDF/XML
node roots retain their subject,
unknown `rdf:parseType` values follow XML-literal fallback semantics, and
valid XML 1.0 Unicode predicate names remain serializable. Property reification
is independent of XML attribute order, including resource and empty/non-empty
collection parse types. Equivalent relative IRI spellings resolve to one visual
resource without WHATWG URL canonicalization. RDF-looking markup inside XML
literals is retained as literal data but excluded from visual projection
discovery. One RDF literal mapped to multiple visual fields updates every
dependent field atomically. Optional derivation metadata also requires an authoritative
`rdf:type owl:Ontology` statement. Imports and SHACL remain inert: external
resources are never fetched and rules are never executed. Actual RDF/XML
`DOCTYPE` declarations and named graph output are rejected explicitly, while
the same text inside comments or character data remains ordinary inert
content. Current resource limits are 8 MiB, 250,000 unique statements, 16,384
characters per expanded RDF IRI-like term, 67,108,864 processed term
characters before deduplication, and 33,554,432 retained term/key characters
per dataset. XML-literal reconstruction applies the same 16,384-character term
limit plus bounded total output and event counts before allocating reconstructed
fragments. Namespace depth tracking avoids copying every inherited declaration
for every element. Input may use UTF-8 or UTF-16; byte signatures, BOMs, and XML
declarations must agree, and unsupported encodings fail explicitly. File
imports reject the declared file size before allocating contents and abort
obsolete reads. The bounded dataset parse must succeed before the main-thread
visual projection starts. Designer editability and statement counts share a
revision-indexed graph cache with dirty-state checks rather than rescanning
large preserved graphs on each render. Async download and share paths verify
the active catalogue entry, source document, initiating component lifetime,
and route before exposing output, while accepting the share route transition
initiated by a successful request. Large complete-source views fall back to one
plain text node instead of constructing an unbounded syntax-token tree; copy
and download still use the complete source.
RDF/XML loaded by URL embeds uses the same preflight and complete-graph parser;
oversized response streams are cancelled before projection.
Catalogue embeds pin a lazy complete-source request to the exact index entry
whose verified payload rendered the graph. If that immutable source artifact
is unavailable, the tab reports the error and keeps generated RDF as the
explicit fallback instead of switching to a newer catalogue version.

For ontologies created in the Playground, exports can use either the
Playground round-trip profile or a standards-oriented OWL + SHACL profile. The
standards profile represents property order, enums, identifiers, relationship
cardinality, and relationship attributes with interoperable vocabulary instead
of treating Playground metadata as Fabric vocabulary. These generated profiles
are not offered for source-backed documents. Modified source exports are
labelled as derived, report source/export statement counts and patch counts,
and can optionally add an explicit `prov:wasDerivedFrom` source-hash statement.
The current Fabric API accepts only the visual projection, so direct Fabric
push is disabled for source-backed documents rather than silently omitting
preserved statements. Download the complete RDF for those documents instead.

Graph rendering graduates automatically with ontology size: small ontologies
remain complete, dense ontologies retain all data with reduced label noise, and
massive ontologies open as a bounded semantic hierarchy overview. Search,
adjustable hop depth, and `+N` boundary expansion keep every hidden entity
reachable without drawing the entire ontology at once. Selecting an entity does
not move the graph; selecting a `+N` entity exposes a neighbor action beside
that node. Expansion keeps existing entities and the viewport anchored while
placing newly revealed hierarchy branches to avoid crossings where possible.
The Semantic overview can hide the selected entity's shown neighborhood again.
When its 180-entity view limit is full it explains which neighbors remain
hidden and asks you to hide a shown neighborhood before expanding another. The
entity legend can be collapsed and automatically starts collapsed when it would
obscure a larger graph. PNG downloads export the currently visible graph within
browser-safe image limits and report failures instead of saving an empty file.
Automated catalogue PR previews wait for the requested graph's completed layout,
independent of whether its legend is collapsed or absent. All node-specific
expansions and the current selection/focus clear when the detail
slider changes, so each hop level starts as an unfocused hierarchy projection
while independent query and path highlights remain visible. Clicking anywhere
clearly to either side of the slider thumb moves to another hop even when the
browser would otherwise round back to the current step; thumb dragging and
arrow keys continue to work normally. Relationship labels stay out of the
overview until an entity is selected, which labels its visible connections, or
an individual relationship is hovered or selected.

Massive graph projections are scheduled and use an interruptible layout so
users can change the semantic view or cancel before or during layout. The Brick
reference case is enforced in a real Chromium run with one initial layout, no
main-thread task or interaction over 200 ms, at most 60 initially rendered
entities, and less than 40 MiB retained JavaScript heap after garbage
collection. Run `npm run build && npm run test:performance` to reproduce the
budget report locally.

Turtle input is not currently supported. See the
[RDF export profiles guide](docs/rdf-export-profiles.md) for the exact
contracts and limitations.

### One-Click Catalogue PR

Sign in with GitHub (device flow) and submit your ontology to the community
catalogue directly from the designer — the app forks the repo, creates a
branch, commits the RDF + metadata, and opens a pull request automatically.
This projection-oriented submission flow is available for Playground-authored
documents; source-backed documents must first be exported and reviewed as a
deliberate derived artifact.

### Embeddable Widget

A self-contained JavaScript file (`ontology-embed.js`) that renders an
interactive ontology viewer on any web page with a single `<script>` tag.
Supports dark/light themes, multiple loading methods (catalogue ID, URL,
inline base64), click-to-inspect, and complete source RDF display/copy for
catalogue and RDF/XML URL sources. URL sources are read with an 8 MiB bound;
RDF/XML URLs also receive the same `DOCTYPE`, statement-count, and inert
resource protections as file imports. The RDF worker is packaged inside the
self-contained embed bundle, so a widget hosted on another HTTPS origin does
not attempt to launch a cross-origin worker script. See the
[Embedding Guide](docs/embed-guide.md) for details.

### Ontology School

A structured learning hub (`/#/learn`) with **9 courses** spanning conceptual
learning paths and hands-on labs:

- **Ontology Fundamentals** — 6 articles covering core concepts (What is an
  Ontology? → RDF/OWL → Fabric IQ → Build Your First → Design Patterns →
  Contributing)
- **7 Domain Learning Paths** — Fourth Coffee, E-Commerce

Quest System

Five progressive quests that guide users through ontology concepts with multi-step instructions, hints, progress bars, and achievement badges.

Natural Language Query Playground

Type natural language questions ("Which customers placed orders?") and see how they map to ontology entities and relationships — a preview of Fabric IQ's NL2Ontology capability.

Command Palette & Keyboard Shortcuts

Press ⌘K / Ctrl+K anywhere to open a searchable command palette. Jump to the Catalogue, Designer, Ontology School, Import/Export, Help, and more without leaving the keyboard. Press ? for quick help access. Arrow keys + Enter to navigate the palette.

Starter Templates

The designer offers five domain templates (Retail, Healthcare, Finance, IoT, Education) so new users never face a blank page. Each template creates 3 entities with properties and 2 relationships, ready to customise.

Interactive Onboarding Tour

First-time visitors get a 5-step guided tour with a spotlight overlay that highlights the Header, Graph, Quests, Inspector, and Designer in sequence. Dismissable with a "don't show again" option persisted to localStorage.

Deep Linking & URL Routing

Client-side hash routing with shareable URLs for every page:

Route Page
/#/ Home (default ontology)
/#/catalogue Ontology gallery
/#/catalogue/<source>/<slug> Specific ontology (e.g. /#/catalogue/official/cosmic-coffee)
/#/designer Visual designer
/#/designer/<source>/<slug> Designer with catalogue ontology (e.g. /#/designer/official/cosmic-coffee)
/#/learn Ontology School — course catalogue
/#/learn/<course> Course detail — article list
/#/learn/<course>/<article> Article view (with presentation mode)

Official Ontologies

Domain Ontology Entities Relationships
Retail Fourth Coffee 6 7
E-Commerce Online Retail 5 6
Healthcare Clinical System 5 6
Finance Banking & Finance 5 6
Manufacturing Industry 4.0 5 5
Education University System 5 6

Getting Started

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 18+
  • npm 9+

Installation

cd Ontology-Playground
npm install

Development

npm run dev

Visit http://localhost:5173

Production Build

npm run build

The build pipeline compiles the catalogue, compiles learning content markdown, type-checks, bundles the app, and builds the embed widget. Output is in build/. The static catalogue output includes catalogue.json, lazy graph payloads under catalogue-payloads/, and byte-preserving originals under catalogue-sources/.

Running Tests

npm test            # single run
npm run test:watch  # watch mode

Validating RDF

npm run validate
npm run validate -- catalogue/external/brick-schema/brick/ontology.rdf
npm run validate -- --profile external path/to/standalone.rdf

Validation discovers all official, community, and external catalogue entries. Official and community entries use the strict Designer profile. External standards use structural, safety, provenance, and resource checks while reporting incompatible Designer conventions as aggregated warnings. Standalone external files require a companion metadata.json; validation never fetches or dereferences external resources.

Deployment

GitHub Pages (official)

The public Ontology Playground is deployed from main to GitHub Pages by .github/workflows/deploy-ghpages.yml. The workflow publishes only the static build/ output; it does not deploy the optional api/ package.

Fork owners can use GitHub Pages by changing the workflow's repository guard, then selecting GitHub Actions under Settings → Pages → Source. The VITE_BASE_PATH environment variable is set to /<repo-name>/ during the build so asset paths resolve correctly. Deployments must retain prior content-addressed files from both catalogue-payloads/ and catalogue-sources/ before replacing the catalogue index so open pages with an older index keep working.

Azure Static Web Apps (optional)

Fork owners may instead host the static frontend with Azure Static Web Apps:

  1. Create a Static Web App in the Azure Portal.
  2. Connect it to your fork.
  3. Add its deployment token as AZURE_STATIC_WEB_APPS_API_TOKEN_GREEN_PLANT_0BB1D2910.
  4. Push to main.

The supplied Azure Static Web Apps workflows also publish static assets only. They do not deploy managed Azure Functions.

Environment Variables

Variable Default Description
VITE_ENABLE_AI_BUILDER false Show the opt-in connector-based AI builder; requires a protected generation gateway
VITE_ENABLE_LEGACY_FORMATS false Enable JSON/YAML/CSV import/export formats
VITE_BASE_PATH / Base path for the app (set automatically for GitHub Pages)
VITE_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID (empty) GitHub OAuth App client ID for one-click catalogue PRs (setup guide)
VITE_GITHUB_OAUTH_BASE (empty) External OAuth proxy URL for GitHub Pages deployments (e.g. Cloudflare Worker URL)
VITE_API_BASE /api Base URL for separately deployed API routes; AI requests must use an authenticated, quota-enforcing gateway

Optional Azure Functions API

The backend in api/ uses the Azure Functions Node.js v4 programming model. It provides the AI ontology builder and the GitHub device-flow OAuth proxy. Azure Functions remains a supported opt-in hosting choice, but it is not part of the official GitHub Pages deployment or any repository-provided deployment workflow. Operators who need these features deploy the Functions app with their own infrastructure and configure the frontend to use that endpoint.

cp api/local.settings.json.template api/local.settings.json
# Replace only the local placeholder values; never commit local.settings.json.
npm --prefix api ci
npm --prefix api run build
npm --prefix api test
npm --prefix api start

AI generation uses an explicit deployment-time connector registry. Azure OpenAI is the reference adapter; operators can add reviewed server-side adapters without changing the builder or core orchestration. There are no remote plugins, request-supplied endpoints, or automatic provider fallbacks.

Generation is disabled by default on both frontend and backend. Both AI Functions now require function keys, intentionally replacing the former anonymous generation route. A function key is not end-user authentication: before enabling this feature, deploy an authenticated, generation-authorizing, quota-enforcing gateway with server-side key injection and block direct backend bypass. Never put function keys or provider secrets in Vite variables, URLs, or browser storage. The repository does not provision this gateway or enable a public AI service.

API route Method Access
/api/generation-connector GET Protected connector disclosure, no provider invocation
/api/generate-ontology POST Protected, identity/revision-pinned generation

Configure AI_CONNECTORS_ENABLED=true, AI_ALLOWED_ORIGIN (one exact frontend origin), and optionally AI_CONNECTOR (default azure-openai) only after the gateway's authentication, CSRF, distributed quotas, and spending controls have been verified. Azure retains AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT, AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY, and AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT (default gpt-4o-mini). The reference adapter accepts only HTTPS resource endpoints under openai.azure.com and rejects credential-bearing redirects.

Set VITE_API_BASE to the protected gateway's /api base and VITE_ENABLE_AI_BUILDER=true to display the builder. Users see the configured provider and processing destination and must consent before a description is submitted. Do not submit secrets or sensitive personal information. Generated output receives server-side shape, size, graph, and Fabric IQ validation; the builder retains preview/edit/apply validation and human review. Generation and edited JSON also require nonempty, Fabric-valid property names unique within each entity. The same name and type may be reused across different entities; incomplete Designer draft editing remains unchanged.

Keep FUNCTIONS_NODE_BLOCK_ON_ENTRY_POINT_ERROR=true so registration failures stop the host. The API compiles the same dependency-free ontology schema and validation helpers used by the frontend; its entry point is dist/api/src/functions/*.js. GitHub OAuth remains separately configured via VITE_GITHUB_OAUTH_BASE; the connector changes do not change its access policy. See Connector authoring and secure deployment for the extension contract, request limits, and mandatory launch checks.

Project Structure

Ontology-Playground/
├── src/
│   ├── components/       # React components (graph, designer, modals, learn page)
│   ├── data/             # Ontology model, query engine, quest definitions
│   ├── lib/              # Router, RDF parser/serializer, catalogue helpers
│   ├── store/            # Zustand stores (app state, designer state)
│   ├── styles/           # CSS (Microsoft Fluent-inspired dark/light themes)
│   └── types/            # TypeScript type definitions
├── catalogue/            # Official + community ontology RDF files
├── content/learn/        # Course directories with markdown articles, quizzes, and metadata
├── scripts/              # Build-time compilers (catalogue, learning content)
├── api/                  # Azure Functions v4 backend (optional)
├── docs/                 # Guides and documentation
├── public/               # Static assets (catalogue index/payloads, learn.json)
└── .github/workflows/    # CI/CD (Azure SWA + GitHub Pages)

Documentation

The table below lists the main end-user and contributor guides. Internal planning notes (for example, docs/TODO-*.md) are intentionally not part of the published documentation set.

Guide Description
Ontology Authoring Guide How to create ontologies that work well in the Playground — field-by-field reference, best practices, and a step-by-step walkthrough
RDF Export Profiles When to use the lossless Playground round-trip profile or the standards-oriented OWL + SHACL profile
Contribute an Ontology: From Design to GitHub End-to-end contributor workflow: design, RDF export, metadata, local validation, and pull request
Embedding Guide How to embed interactive ontology widgets on any web page
Generating RDF from External Tools Current RDF/XML import subset, typed descriptions, native subclass axioms, and source-artifact versus generated-subset limits for external generators
GitHub OAuth Setup How to configure GitHub OAuth for one-click catalogue PRs
Embed Security Security model for the embeddable widget
Learning Content Guide How to author courses, articles, quizzes, and ontology embeds for the Ontology School
Ontology School Review Workflow Human review and approval flow for school lesson content
Theme Authoring Guide How to plug a new color theme into the Playground — token contract, the appStore + CSS steps, and contrast gotchas

AI Agent Quickstart

This repository includes Copilot customization files so agents can reliably:

  • import customer RDF/OWL into catalogue-ready format
  • generate progressive Ontology School modules
  • route lesson content through human review workflows

Included assets:

  • Skills:
    • .github/skills/ontology-catalog-import/ — import external/customer RDF/OWL into catalogue format
    • .github/skills/ontology-school-path-generator/ — generate progressive Ontology School modules
    • .github/skills/community-ontology-contribution/ — add a contributor ontology under catalogue/community/ with the correct directory structure, metadata, and validation
    • .github/skills/name-generator/ — generate person names for examples, demos, quests, tests, and sample data from the approved CSV fixture
  • RDF intake instruction:
    • .github/instructions/rdf-intake.instructions.md
  • Reusable prompts:
    • .github/prompts/import-rdf-to-catalog.prompt.md
    • .github/prompts/generate-ontology-school-module.prompt.md

Recommended validation before merge:

npm run qa:tutorial-content
npm run build

Technologies

  • React 19 + TypeScript 5
  • Cytoscape.js — Graph visualization (fcose layout)
  • Zustand — State management
  • Vite — Build tool
  • Framer Motion — Animations
  • Lucide Icons — Icon library
  • marked — Markdown compilation (build-time)

aiSummary.oneLiner: An interactive environment for visualizing, editing, and validating complex knowledge graphs and ontologies.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: Ontology Playground offers a highly visual, interactive web interface designed for constructing, exploring, and rigorously validating complex semantic ontologies, specifically optimized for Microsoft Fabric IQ. It abstracts the immense complexity of raw RDF or OWL files by providing an intuitive node-based graph editor. Users can easily define intricate entity relationships, set strict property constraints, and instantly visualize the entire resulting knowledge structure in real-time. The tool includes a curated catalogue of industry ontologies, real-time schema validation, and full round-trip export capabilities to standard RDF/XML formats.
keyFeatures: Visual graph editing: Allows users to construct and modify complex ontologies using a highly intuitive, drag-and-drop node interface powered by Cytoscape.js.
Interactive exploration: Renders any ontology as a clickable diagram where users can pan, zoom, and inspect detailed entity properties.
Ontology catalogue: Provides a curated, searchable library of pre-built official and community-contributed ontologies spanning multiple industries.
RDF Import/Export: Fully supports importing and exporting standard RDF/XML files without losing object properties or cardinalities.
One-click PRs: Enables users to submit new ontologies to the official community catalogue directly from the designer via GitHub device flow.
